title: Rework streaming token loop and flush cadence to reduce tail latency
author: Anya Kapoor
description: Motivation: streaming responses in production exhibited high 95/99th token latency under common microburst traffic. Root causes identified: (1) token generation loop used blocking flush cadence that batched too aggressively for low-latency clients, (2) backpressure from synchronous KV cache writes and global locks, and (3) kernel scheduling favored throughput over rapid token dispatch. This PR reworks the token loop to be event-driven with adaptive flush cadence, adds non-blocking async KV cache writes with lock striping, and introduces a fast-path scheduler for streaming sessions. Changes are gated behind feature flag `streaming-low-latency` and rolled out as a canary on the perf-canary cluster before wider rollout. Checklist: - [x] Profiling and root cause writeup attached - [x] Token loop rewrite + unit tests - [x] Async KV cache + integration tests - [x] Scheduler fast-path + e2e canary run - [x] Documentation: runtime tuning guide updated - [x] Feature flag and rollout plan described in PR body What changed (high level): - Token loop: converted from synchronous loop that flushed after accumulating N tokens or T ms to an event-driven loop that flushes immediately when forward pass completes and adaptively relaxes batching for longer sequences. Introduced a minimum flush cadence default of 12ms (previously effectively 50-100ms under microburst batching) and a jittered backoff to avoid synchronized flush storms. - Backpressure/backoff: replaced global request queue backpressure with per-session credit buckets so a slow client doesn't stall unrelated sessions. Token emission now respects a per-session soft-rate and hard-rate fallback. - KV cache: writes are now async and use lock striping per-key-shard; synchronous fence at end-of-stream only when necessary. Reads keep existing consistency model; we prefetch adjacent KV shards when sequence length grows to reduce miss penalty. - Scheduler: added a low-latency fast-path that prioritizes streaming sessions with small outstanding batch sizes and pins them to warm kernels; throughput scheduling unchanged for bulk inference. - Kernel/kernels selection: added a micro-batch kernel path that targets single-token forward when sequence window is small, reducing kernel invocation overhead. - Observability: new metrics (stream.flush_latency_ms, stream.flush_count, stream.backpressure_sessions) and dashboards added; traces include token loop stalls. Testing and results: - Unit and integration test suites updated; new harness for simulated slow clients. - Canary run (perf-canary cluster) across 200 concurrent streaming sessions with mix of short/long sequences. Results vs main baseline: median token-to-token latency: -12.5% (from 8.0ms to 7.0ms), p50 latency -12.5%; p95 token latency: -28% (from 34ms to 24.5ms); p99 token latency: -32% (from 92ms to 62.5ms). End-to-end streaming tail (95th percentile response time for 128-token responses) improved ~18%. Cost impact: slight increase in GPU kernels invoked (micro-batch path) but offset by reduced prefix replays and improved batching heuristics; net token cost estimated to be within +/-1% in our workload mix. Rollout plan: enable `streaming-low-latency` for internal canaries -> stage in one region -> monitor stream metrics and error budget for 72h -> gradual ramp to 100% if stable. If regressions seen, rollback to main via feature flag. Backwards compatibility: no API-level changes; default behavior unchanged unless feature flag is enabled. Notes on potential regressions: throughput-sensitive batch jobs could see small throughput regression; operator docs updated with knob guidance to disable fast-path for throughput-critical queues. Related: ENG-7421 (token loop redesign), ENG-7589 (kv cache async writes).
